question.problem:
A stick of length $6$ is broken at a point chosen uniformly at random along its length. Let the continuous random variable $X$ denote the distance from the left end of the stick to the break point, and let $Y=Y(X)$ denote the length of the shortest piece.

Expressing the integrands in the following equation as polynomials, we have

$\text{E}[Y]={\int }_{0}^{3}$
{{field-1}} $\text{d}x\,\,+\,\,{\int }_{3}^{6}$
{{field-2}} $\text{d}x$

Therefore, the expected length of the shorter piece is  
{{field-3}}.
question.worked_solution:
For a continuous random variable $X$ and a function $r(x)$, the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(x)]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }r(x)f(x)\text{ }\text{d}x,
$$

where $f(x)$ is the probability density function of $X.$ 

In this problem, the break point $X$ is chosen uniformly from $[0,6]$, so the probability density function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{6},\,\,\,\,\,\,0\le x<6.
$$

When the stick is broken at point $X$, it is divided into two pieces: one of length $X$ and the other of length $6-X.$ The shorter of the two pieces, $Y$, is therefore given by

$$
Y=\text{min}(X,6-X).
$$

Therefore, we define

$$
r(x)=\text{min}(x,6-x).
$$

To evaluate the integral, we express $r(x)$ as an explicit piecewise function. Observe that,

- if $0\le x<3$, then $x<6-x$, so the shorter piece has length $x$,

- if $3\le x\le 6$, then $x\ge 6-x$, so the shorter piece has length $6-x.$

Therefore,

$$
r(x)=\{\begin{aligned}x, & 0\le x<3, \\ 6-x, & 3\le x\le 6.\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =\text{E}[\text{min}(X,6-X)] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }r(x)f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}x\cdot \frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{6}(6-x)\cdot \frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}x\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{3}^{6}(6-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{3}+\frac{1}{6}{[6x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{3}^{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(\frac{9}{2})+\frac{1}{6}[(36-18)-(18-\frac{9}{2})] \\  & =\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{6}(18-\frac{27}{2}) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{6}(\frac{9}{2}) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}+\frac{3}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the expected length of the shorter piece is $\frac{3}{2}.$
